correctness.rationale: For an identifiable canonical threshold graph, the closed neighborhoods are \(N[z]=\{z\}\cup\{d_i,\ldots,d_k\}\) for \(z\in Z_i\) and \(N[d_i]=\{d_1,\ldots,d_k\}\cup Z_1\cup\cdots\cup Z_i\). These formulas make every possible code-trace collision explicit. Same-block zero vertices force at most one omission; singleton later zero blocks cannot be omitted because they would identify consecutive \(d\)-vertices; when \(a_1=2\), one omission identifies the remaining \(Z_1\)-vertex with \(d_1\). Omitted zero vertices in distinct eligible blocks are separated exactly by selected \(d\)-vertices in the intervening index interval, and the final omitted zero vertex is dominated exactly by a selected \(d\)-vertex in the final interval. These conditions are sufficient by an exhaustive pair-type argument. The generating function follows from independent selection on disjoint required intervals. A direct brute-force checker matches every coefficient for 511 connected canonical threshold strings through order 10, totaling 349524 subset tests; this finite check corroborates but does not replace the proof.

value.rationale: Threshold graphs are a canonical hereditary subclass of split graphs with a compact creation-string representation, whereas identifying-code optimization is hard on split graphs in general. The result gives a natural complete structural classification, an exact existence criterion, the full cardinality generating polynomial, the minimum size, and the exact number of minimum codes. The disjoint interval-hitting representation exposes why the threshold subclass is tractable and is useful for enumeration rather than merely recomputing one small invariant.
